Daniel.line: Daniel and his friends stay faithful to God in exile, and Daniel receives visions of God's rule over the world's kingdoms.
more: Chapters 1–6 tell stories of Daniel and his friends serving under Babylonian and Persian kings.
God gives Daniel wisdom to interpret dreams and preserves his servants in the fiery furnace and the lions' den.
Proud kings like Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar learn that the Most High rules over human kingdoms.
Chapters 7–12 record Daniel's visions of beasts, kingdoms, and an everlasting kingdom given to one like a son of man.
The book closes with a long vision of coming conflicts, the resurrection, and a final word to Daniel.

1.line: Daniel and three Judean friends are taken to Babylon, refuse the king's food, and prove healthier and wiser than all others.
more: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem and has young Judean nobles trained for royal service.
They receive Babylonian names: Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
After ten days on vegetables and water, they look healthier than those eating the king's food.
God gives them learning and wisdom, and gives Daniel understanding of visions and dreams.

2.line: Daniel tells and interprets Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a great statue destroyed by a stone that becomes a mountain.
more: The king demands that his wise men tell him the dream itself, or die.
God reveals the dream to Daniel in a night vision after he and his friends pray.
The statue's metal parts represent successive kingdoms; the stone is a kingdom God will set up forever.
Nebuchadnezzar honors Daniel's God and promotes Daniel and his friends.

3.line: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and survive being thrown into a fiery furnace.
more: Nebuchadnezzar orders all officials to bow to a huge golden image on the plain of Dura.
The three friends say God can deliver them, but they will not serve other gods regardless.
The king sees four men walking unharmed in the fire, the fourth like a son of the gods.
Nebuchadnezzar praises their God and forbids anyone to speak against him.

4.line: Nebuchadnezzar recounts how his pride led to madness until he acknowledged that the Most High rules over human kingdoms.
more: He dreams of a great tree cut down, leaving only a stump bound with iron and bronze.
Daniel explains that the king will live like an animal until he recognizes God's rule.
A year later, while boasting over Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar is driven out to live among beasts.
When his reason returns, he praises God and is restored to his kingdom.

5.line: During King Belshazzar's feast, a hand writes on the wall, Daniel interprets it, and Babylon falls that night.
more: Belshazzar drinks from vessels taken from Jerusalem's temple while praising gods of gold and silver.
The queen recommends Daniel, who rebukes the king for not humbling himself as Nebuchadnezzar did.
The words mean that God has numbered, weighed, and divided Belshazzar's kingdom.
Belshazzar is killed that night, and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom.

6.line: Daniel keeps praying to God despite a royal ban, is thrown into the lions' den, and God shuts the lions' mouths.
more: Jealous officials persuade King Darius to sign a thirty-day decree forbidding prayer to anyone but him.
Darius is distressed but cannot revoke the law and has Daniel thrown to the lions.
At dawn Daniel is found unharmed, and his accusers are thrown into the den instead.
Darius decrees that all should fear the living God of Daniel.

7.line: Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea, then the Ancient of Days giving everlasting dominion to one like a son of man.
more: The beasts resemble a lion, a bear, a leopard, and a terrifying beast with ten horns.
A little horn speaks boastfully and makes war on the saints for a time.
The Ancient of Days sits in judgment, and the fourth beast is destroyed.
Daniel is told the beasts are kingdoms, and the kingdom will be given to the saints of the Most High.

8.line: Daniel sees a ram and a goat, which Gabriel explains represent Media-Persia, Greece, and a later arrogant king.
more: A two-horned ram is trampled by a goat whose prominent horn is then broken.
Four horns replace it, and from one a little horn grows and halts the regular burnt offering.
The sanctuary is to be restored after 2,300 evenings and mornings.
Gabriel says the vision concerns the time of the end, and Daniel is left exhausted and appalled.

9.line: Daniel confesses Israel's sins and prays for Jerusalem, and Gabriel brings a revelation of seventy weeks.
more: Reading Jeremiah, Daniel understands that Jerusalem's desolation will last seventy years.
He confesses that Israel has sinned and deserves judgment, and appeals to God's mercy and name.
Gabriel says seventy weeks are decreed to end sin, bring everlasting righteousness, and anoint a most holy place.
He speaks of an anointed one cut off, the city destroyed, and an abomination that makes desolate.

10.line: After three weeks of mourning, Daniel sees a glorious heavenly messenger who comes to explain what will happen to his people.
more: In Cyrus's third year, Daniel fasts and then stands beside the Tigris River.
He sees a man clothed in linen, with a face like lightning, and falls into a deep sleep.
The messenger says the prince of Persia opposed him until Michael came to help.
He strengthens Daniel and prepares to reveal what is written in the book of truth.

11.line: The messenger foretells conflicts among Persian and Greek kings, the kings of the north and south, and a contemptible ruler.
more: Persian kings will be followed by a mighty king whose kingdom is divided four ways.
The kings of the south and the north will wage long wars and make failed alliances.
A contemptible king will profane the temple, end the regular offering, and set up the abomination of desolation.
Those who know their God will stand firm, and the king will exalt himself until his end.

12.line: The vision ends with a time of trouble, the deliverance of God's people, the resurrection, and instructions to seal the book.
more: Michael will arise, and everyone whose name is written in the book will be delivered.
Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life, others to everlasting contempt.
Daniel is told to seal the book until the time of the end.
He is promised rest and that he will rise to his allotted place at the end.

Hosea.line: Through Hosea's marriage to an unfaithful wife, God exposes Israel's spiritual adultery and promises a love that will restore them.
more: Hosea prophesies to the northern kingdom of Israel in its final decades before Assyria conquers it.
God commands Hosea to marry Gomer, whose unfaithfulness pictures Israel's worship of Baal.
Most of the book indicts Israel for idolatry, injustice, foreign alliances, and lack of knowledge of God.
Judgment is announced, yet God repeatedly declares his compassion for his people.
The book ends with a call to return and promises of healing and renewal.

1.line: God commands Hosea to marry Gomer, and their three children receive names announcing judgment on Israel.
more: The marriage pictures Israel committing great whoredom by forsaking the LORD.
Jezreel signals punishment for the house of Jehu, and Lo-ruhamah means no mercy.
Lo-ammi means not my people, declaring a broken covenant relationship.
Yet God promises that Israel and Judah will be numerous and reunited under one head.

2.line: God charges Israel as an unfaithful wife, promises to strip her, then to win her back and renew the covenant.
more: Israel credits her lovers, the Baals, with grain, wine, and oil that God provided.
God will block her paths, take back his gifts, and end her festivals.
He will allure her into the wilderness and speak tenderly, and she will call him her husband.
He will betroth her forever in righteousness and faithfulness, and call not my people his people.

3.line: God tells Hosea to love his adulterous wife again, picturing his love for Israel despite their idolatry.
more: Hosea buys her back for silver and barley.
She must stay with him many days without other men.
Likewise Israel will live many days without king, sacrifice, or idols.
Afterward Israel will return and seek the LORD and David their king in the latter days.

4.line: The LORD brings a charge against Israel for lacking faithfulness, love, and knowledge of God, and blames the priests.
more: Swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and adultery fill the land, and the land mourns.
The people are destroyed for lack of knowledge because the priests rejected it.
They consult wooden idols and practice cult prostitution on the hilltops.
Judah is warned not to share Israel's guilt.

5.line: God announces judgment on Israel's priests, people, and royal house, and on Judah too, for their pride and unfaithfulness.
more: Their deeds keep them from returning to God, and their pride testifies against them.
The alarm sounds as God becomes like a moth and a lion to Ephraim and Judah.
Ephraim turns to Assyria for help, but Assyria cannot heal him.
God will withdraw until they acknowledge their guilt and seek him.

6.line: Israel speaks of returning to the LORD, but God laments that their love vanishes like morning mist.
more: The people expect God to heal and revive them after two days.
God says their love is like a cloud or dew that goes away early.
He desires steadfast love and knowledge of God rather than sacrifices and burnt offerings.
Like Adam they transgressed the covenant, and even priests commit violence.

7.line: God describes Israel's corruption, political intrigue, and foreign alliances, and laments that they do not cry out to him.
more: Their leaders burn with intrigue like an oven, and their kings fall.
Ephraim is like a half-baked cake, mixed with the nations and unaware of his decline.
Like a senseless dove, Israel calls to Egypt and goes to Assyria.
God would redeem them, but they speak lies against him and turn away.

8.line: Israel has broken the covenant by making kings and idols without God, and will reap the whirlwind.
more: They set up kings and princes without God's approval.
The calf of Samaria will be broken to pieces.
They sow the wind, and they hire lovers among the nations.
Their many altars have become places for sinning, and they will return to Egypt.

9.line: Hosea announces that Israel's festivals will end in exile because they have played the whore and rejected God's prophets.
more: They will not remain in the LORD's land but return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria.
The days of punishment have come, and the prophet is considered a fool.
Israel was once like grapes in the wilderness, but they consecrated themselves to Baal at Baal-peor.
Their fruitfulness will fail, and they will become wanderers among the nations.

10.line: Israel's prosperity has increased their idolatry, so their altars, calf, and king will be destroyed.
more: As their fruit increased, they built more altars and pillars.
The calf of Beth-aven will be carried to Assyria, and Samaria's king will perish.
God calls them to sow righteousness and seek the LORD.
Because they trusted in their own way and warriors, war will destroy their fortresses.

11.line: God recalls loving Israel as a child from Egypt and, despite their rebellion, refuses to destroy them completely.
more: He called his son out of Egypt, taught Ephraim to walk, and led them with kindness.
Yet they kept sacrificing to the Baals, so Assyria will rule over them.
God's heart recoils within him, and he will not execute his burning anger.
His people will come trembling from Egypt and Assyria, and he will return them home.

12.line: God brings an indictment against Ephraim and Judah, recalling Jacob's life and Israel's deceit and dishonest trade.
more: Ephraim makes a covenant with Assyria and carries oil to Egypt.
Jacob strove with God and wept, seeking favor, and met God at Bethel.
Israel is called to return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait for God.
Ephraim boasts of riches gained by false balances, so God will repay him.

13.line: Ephraim, once exalted, has turned to Baal and calf idols, so God will come against them like a wild beast.
more: They make silver idols and kiss calves.
God cared for them in the wilderness, but when they were full, they forgot him.
Their king cannot save them, and Samaria will bear her guilt and fall by the sword.
God speaks of the power of Sheol and death, asking where their plagues and sting are.

14.line: Hosea calls Israel to return to the LORD with words of repentance, and God promises to heal and love them freely.
more: Israel is to confess that Assyria cannot save them and that they will not worship idols.
God will heal their apostasy, and his anger has turned away.
Israel will flourish like a lily, an olive tree, and the cedars of Lebanon.
The wise will understand that the ways of the LORD are right.

Joel.line: Joel uses a devastating locust plague to call Judah to repentance and to announce the coming day of the LORD.
more: A locust invasion has stripped the land, and Joel calls everyone to mourn and seek God.
He describes the day of the LORD as an army advancing against Judah.
God calls his people to return with all their hearts and promises to restore what was lost.
He promises to pour out his Spirit on all flesh.
The nations will be judged in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, while Judah and Jerusalem are blessed forever.

1.line: Joel describes a locust plague that has devastated Judah and calls priests and people to fast and cry out to God.
more: Successive swarms of locusts have eaten what the others left.
Vines, fig trees, and fields are ruined, and grain and drink offerings are cut off.
Priests are told to put on sackcloth and call a solemn assembly.
Joel warns that the day of the LORD is near, and even the animals groan for pasture.

2.line: The day of the LORD comes like an invading army, but God calls Judah to repent and promises restoration and his Spirit.
more: A great people runs like horses and scales walls, and the LORD leads his army.
God calls them to return with fasting and to rend their hearts, not garments, for he is gracious.
He will send grain, wine, and oil, and restore the years the locusts ate.
Afterward he will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and everyone who calls on his name will be saved.

3.line: God will gather the nations for judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat and dwell in Zion with his restored people.
more: He will judge the nations for scattering Israel and dividing his land.
Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia are condemned for selling his people and plundering his treasures.
The nations are summoned to beat plowshares into swords for battle in the valley of decision.
Jerusalem will be holy, the mountains will drip sweet wine, and Egypt and Edom will become desolate.

Amos.line: Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa, warns prosperous Israel that God will judge their injustice, empty worship, and complacency.
more: Amos prophesies in the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel.
He opens with judgments on surrounding nations, then turns to Judah and Israel.
He condemns oppression of the poor, corrupt courts, luxury, and religion without righteousness.
Five visions show approaching judgment, and the priest Amaziah orders Amos to leave Bethel.
The book ends with a promise to restore David's fallen booth and replant Israel in their land.

1.line: The LORD roars from Zion and announces judgment on Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon for their crimes.
more: Amos receives these words two years before the earthquake.
Each oracle begins with a formula of three transgressions and four, introducing the nation's crime.
The crimes include cruelty in war, selling captives as slaves, and breaking a covenant of brotherhood.
God will send fire on their strongholds and exile their rulers.

2.line: God's judgment extends to Moab, Judah, and finally Israel, whose oppression of the poor and immorality will be punished.
more: Moab burned the bones of Edom's king, and Judah rejected the law of the LORD.
Israel sells the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.
God recalls destroying the Amorites, bringing Israel out of Egypt, and raising prophets and Nazirites.
No one, not even the swiftest or bravest, will escape the coming judgment.

3.line: Because God chose Israel, he will punish them for all their iniquities, and Samaria's strongholds and Bethel's altars will fall.
more: A series of questions shows that the prophet speaks because the LORD has spoken.
Neighboring nations are summoned to witness the oppression in Samaria.
Only a remnant will be rescued, like pieces of a lamb snatched from a lion.
The horns of Bethel's altar will be cut off, and fine houses will perish.

4.line: God condemns the wealthy women of Samaria and Israel's empty worship, and recounts disasters that failed to bring them back.
more: The cows of Bashan oppress the poor and demand drinks from their husbands.
Israel loves to offer sacrifices at Bethel and Gilgal, yet keeps sinning.
Famine, drought, blight, plague, and overthrow came, yet they did not return to God.
Therefore Israel must prepare to meet its God.

5.line: Amos laments Israel's coming fall and calls them to seek the LORD, establish justice, and stop trusting in empty worship.
more: God tells them to seek him and live, not to seek Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba.
Israel turns justice to wormwood, taxes the poor, and takes bribes.
The day of the LORD will be darkness, not light, for those who long for it.
God rejects their festivals and wants justice to roll down like waters.

6.line: God pronounces woe on the complacent leaders of Zion and Samaria, who live in luxury while ignoring the nation's ruin.
more: They lounge on ivory beds, feast, and drink wine from bowls.
They are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph.
They will be the first to go into exile, and their revelry will end.
God will raise up a nation to oppress Israel from one end to the other.

7.line: Amos sees visions of locusts, fire, and a plumb line, and the priest Amaziah orders him to leave Bethel.
more: Amos intercedes after the locust and fire visions, and the LORD relents.
The plumb line shows God will no longer pass by Israel, and Jeroboam's house will fall.
Amaziah reports Amos to King Jeroboam and tells him to prophesy in Judah instead.
Amos replies that he was a herdsman called by God, and foretells Amaziah's ruin and Israel's exile.

8.line: A vision of summer fruit signals Israel's end, as God condemns merchants who cheat the poor.
more: The end has come, and songs in the temple will become wailing.
Merchants impatient for the Sabbath to end use false scales and buy the needy.
God swears he will never forget their deeds, and the land will tremble.
He will send a famine of hearing the words of the LORD.

9.line: Amos sees the LORD at the altar decreeing inescapable judgment, followed by a promise to restore David's fallen booth.
more: No one can hide from God, whether in Sheol, heaven, Carmel, or the sea.
God will shake Israel like a sieve, and the sinners among his people will die by the sword.
He will raise up David's booth and rebuild its ruins.
Israel will rebuild cities, plant vineyards, and never again be uprooted from their land.

Obadiah.line: Obadiah announces God's judgment on Edom for its pride and violence against Judah, and promises Israel's restoration.
more: Edom trusts its high mountain strongholds, but God will bring it down.
Its allies will betray it, and its wise men will be destroyed.
Edom is condemned for gloating, looting, and handing over survivors when Jerusalem fell.
The day of the LORD will repay the nations, and Mount Zion will rule over Esau.

1.line: The vision of Obadiah condemns Edom for violence against its brother Jacob and declares that the kingdom will be the LORD's.
more: Though Edom nests among the stars, God will bring it down and plunder its treasures.
Edom stood aloof and rejoiced when strangers entered Jerusalem.
As Edom has done, so it will be done to Edom.
Exiles of Israel will possess Edom and surrounding lands, and saviors will rule from Mount Zion.

Jonah.line: God sends the reluctant prophet Jonah to warn Nineveh, spares the repentant city, and confronts Jonah's anger over his mercy.
more: Jonah flees toward Tarshish, and God sends a storm that stops him.
Thrown overboard, he is swallowed by a great fish and prays for deliverance.
He preaches in Nineveh, and the whole city repents.
God relents from disaster and uses a plant to question Jonah's resentment.

1.line: Jonah flees from God's call to Nineveh by ship, and a great storm leads the sailors to throw him overboard.
more: Jonah boards a ship at Joppa bound for Tarshish.
The terrified sailors cry to their gods, and the lot falls on Jonah.
Jonah confesses that he fears the LORD, who made the sea and the dry land.
When they throw him overboard, the sea calms, and the LORD appoints a great fish to swallow him.

2.line: From inside the great fish, Jonah prays a psalm of thanks for God's rescue, and the fish vomits him onto land.
more: Jonah describes sinking into the deep, surrounded by waters and seaweed.
He remembered the LORD, and God brought his life up from the pit.
He vows to sacrifice and declares that salvation belongs to the LORD.
Jonah was in the fish three days and three nights.

3.line: Jonah proclaims Nineveh's coming overthrow, the city repents, and God relents from the disaster.
more: God calls Jonah a second time, and he obeys.
He warns that in forty days Nineveh will be overthrown.
The people believe God, and the king orders fasting, sackcloth, and turning from violence.
God sees their repentance and does not bring the threatened disaster.

4.line: Jonah is angry at God's mercy, and God uses a plant to show him why he cares for Nineveh.
more: Jonah says he fled because he knew God is gracious and relents from disaster.
God appoints a plant to shade him, then a worm to destroy it.
Jonah, angry about the plant, wishes to die.
God asks whether he should not pity Nineveh, with its many people and animals.

Micah.line: Micah announces judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem for idolatry and injustice, and promises a coming ruler and restoration.
more: Micah prophesies in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.
He condemns corrupt rulers, greedy landowners, false prophets, and bribed priests.
He foresees Zion exalted and a ruler from Bethlehem who will shepherd God's people.
God brings a case against Israel and declares what he requires: justice, kindness, and humility.
The book ends with confidence in God's pardon and his faithfulness to Abraham and Jacob.

1.line: The LORD comes in judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem, and Micah laments the disaster coming to Judah.
more: Mountains melt beneath God as he comes down from his holy place.
Samaria will become a heap of ruins, and its idols will be beaten to pieces.
Micah goes stripped and wailing because the wound has reached Jerusalem's gate.
Using wordplay on town names, he describes judgment spreading through Judah's towns.

2.line: Micah condemns those who seize fields and houses and reject true prophecy, then promises God will gather a remnant.
more: Schemers plot at night and seize land, so God plans disaster against them.
People tell Micah not to preach, preferring a prophet who speaks of wine.
They rob peaceful travelers and evict women and children from their homes.
God will gather the remnant of Israel like sheep, with their king leading them.

3.line: Micah denounces Israel's rulers, prophets, and priests for corruption, declaring that Zion will be plowed like a field.
more: Rulers who should know justice hate good and devour the people.
Prophets cry peace when fed and declare war on those who feed them nothing.
Micah is filled with power by the Spirit to declare Israel's sin.
Leaders judge for bribes yet claim the LORD is with them.

4.line: In the latter days, the LORD's mountain will be exalted, nations will learn his ways, and he will restore his scattered people.
more: Nations will stream to Zion and beat their swords into plowshares.
Everyone will sit under his vine and fig tree without fear.
God will gather the lame and the exiled and reign over them in Zion.
Zion must go to Babylon but will be rescued and will thresh the nations.

5.line: A ruler from Bethlehem will come to shepherd Israel in the LORD's strength, and his remnant will triumph.
more: Though Israel's judge is struck, a ruler whose origin is from of old will come.
He will stand and shepherd his flock, and he will be their peace.
The remnant of Jacob will be like dew among peoples and like a lion among beasts.
God will remove horses, chariots, sorcery, and idols, and take vengeance on disobedient nations.

6.line: The LORD brings a case against Israel, declares what he requires, and condemns Israel's dishonesty and violence.
more: God recalls redeeming Israel from Egypt and sending Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
He requires not thousands of offerings but doing justice, loving kindness, and walking humbly with him.
The city is full of false scales, violence, and lies.
Because they follow the ways of Omri and Ahab, they will eat and not be satisfied.

7.line: Micah mourns the moral collapse of society, waits for God's salvation, and praises God who pardons sin.
more: The godly have perished, and even family members have become enemies.
Micah will look to the LORD and wait for God, who will bring him to the light.
Walls will be rebuilt, and nations will see God's wonders and be ashamed.
God will cast all sins into the sea and show faithfulness to Jacob and Abraham.

Nahum.line: Nahum announces God's judgment on Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, and comforts Judah with news of its downfall.
more: The LORD is slow to anger but will not leave the guilty unpunished.
He is a stronghold for those who take refuge in him and an end for his enemies.
Nahum vividly describes the attack and plunder of Nineveh.
Assyria's cruelty and deceit bring its doom, and those who hear the news clap their hands.

1.line: Nahum describes the LORD as a jealous, avenging God who will destroy Nineveh and free Judah from its yoke.
more: The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, and mountains quake before him.
He is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble for those who trust him.
Nineveh's plots will end, and its name and idols will be cut off.
A messenger brings good news of peace, and Judah is told to keep its feasts.

2.line: Nahum depicts an attacking army storming Nineveh, plundering its wealth, and leaving the lions' den empty.
more: Red-clad warriors and flashing chariots race through the streets.
The river gates open, the palace melts, and Nineveh's people flee.
Its silver and gold are plundered, and hearts melt in terror.
Nineveh, once a den of lions filled with prey, will be cut off by the LORD.

3.line: Woe is pronounced on Nineveh, a bloody city of lies and sorcery, whose fall will be complete and unmourned.
more: Charging horsemen leave heaps of corpses in the city.
God will expose Nineveh's shame before the nations like a prostitute's.
Like Thebes, which fell despite its defenses, Nineveh will not escape.
Its fortresses and troops will fail, and all who hear of its end will clap their hands.

Habakkuk.line: Habakkuk questions God about injustice and the coming Babylonian invasion, and learns to trust and rejoice in God.
more: Habakkuk complains that violence and injustice go unpunished in Judah.
God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans to bring judgment.
Habakkuk asks how a holy God can use a wicked nation, and waits for an answer.
God says the righteous will live by faith and pronounces woes on the proud oppressor.
Habakkuk's closing prayer recalls God's mighty deeds and resolves to rejoice even in loss.

1.line: Habakkuk complains that God tolerates injustice, and God answers that he is raising up the Babylonians to judge Judah.
more: The prophet asks how long he must cry for help while violence goes on.
God describes the Chaldeans as fierce, swift, and a law to themselves.
Habakkuk asks why a holy God would let the wicked swallow those more righteous.
He pictures the invader catching people like fish in a net and sacrificing to his net.

2.line: God tells Habakkuk to record the vision, says the righteous will live by faith, and pronounces five woes on the oppressor.
more: Habakkuk stations himself on the watchtower to await God's reply.
The vision awaits its appointed time and will surely come.
Woes fall on plunder, unjust gain, bloodshed, shaming neighbors, and idolatry.
The earth will be filled with knowledge of the LORD's glory, and the LORD is in his holy temple.

3.line: Habakkuk prays for God to act, recalls his mighty deeds, and resolves to rejoice in God even if crops fail.
more: He asks God to revive his work and remember mercy in wrath.
He portrays God coming in splendor, shaking the earth and defeating enemies to save his people.
Hearing this, Habakkuk trembles yet waits quietly for the day of trouble to come on the invaders.
Though fig trees and fields fail, he will rejoice in the God of his salvation.

Zephaniah.line: Zephaniah warns Judah and the nations of the coming day of the LORD and promises joy for a humble remnant.
more: Zephaniah prophesies during the reign of Josiah king of Judah.
He announces sweeping judgment on Judah for idolatry and complacency.
He calls the humble to seek the LORD and pronounces judgment on surrounding nations.
Jerusalem's corrupt leaders are condemned, yet God promises to purify the peoples.
The book ends with God rejoicing over a restored Zion.

1.line: Zephaniah announces that the day of the LORD will sweep away Judah's idolaters and complacent people.
more: God will consume everything from the face of the earth, people and animals alike.
He will cut off Baal worship, idolatrous priests, and those who swear by Milcom.
He will search Jerusalem with lamps and punish those who say God does nothing.
The great day of the LORD is near, a day of wrath, distress, and darkness.

2.line: Zephaniah urges the humble to seek the LORD and announces judgment on Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria.
more: Seeking righteousness and humility may hide them on the day of the LORD's anger.
The remnant of Judah will possess the Philistine coast and the lands of Moab and Ammon.
Moab and Ammon will become like Sodom and Gomorrah for taunting God's people.
Nineveh, the exultant city, will become a desolate place for wild animals.

3.line: God condemns Jerusalem's rebellious leaders but promises to purify the nations and rejoice over a restored remnant in Zion.
more: Jerusalem's officials, judges, prophets, and priests are corrupt and do not trust the LORD.
God will change the peoples' speech so all may call on his name.
A humble remnant will do no injustice and will seek refuge in the LORD.
God will rejoice over Zion with singing, gather the outcasts, and restore their fortunes.

Haggai.line: Haggai urges the returned exiles to rebuild the temple and promises God's presence, glory, and blessing.
more: Haggai prophesies in the second year of Darius to Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people.
The people have neglected the temple while building their own houses.
Leaders and people respond and resume the work.
God promises that the new temple's glory will exceed the former and announces blessing from that day.
Zerubbabel is chosen as God's signet ring.

1.line: Haggai rebukes the people for neglecting the temple, and Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people obey and begin rebuilding.
more: The people say it is not yet time, while living in paneled houses.
Their harvests and wages fail because God's house lies in ruins.
God tells them to bring wood and build so he may be glorified.
The LORD stirs up their spirits, and they work on his house.

2.line: Haggai encourages the builders with promises of future glory, warns of impurity, and announces blessing and Zerubbabel's chosen role.
more: Though the new temple seems as nothing, God says his Spirit remains among them.
He will shake the nations, and the latter glory of the house will be greater.
Questions about holiness show the people's offerings were unclean, but blessing begins now.
God will overthrow kingdoms and make Zerubbabel like a signet ring.

Zechariah.line: Zechariah encourages the returned exiles through visions and oracles about rebuilding the temple and God's coming king and kingdom.
more: Zechariah begins prophesying in Darius's second year with a call to return to the LORD.
Eight night visions show God's care for Jerusalem, judgment on nations, and the cleansing of sin.
Joshua the high priest is crowned, pointing to the Branch who will build the temple.
A question about fasting leads to calls for justice and promises of joy in Zion.
Later oracles announce a humble king, a rejected shepherd, a pierced one, and the LORD's reign over all the earth.

1.line: Zechariah calls the people to return to the LORD and sees visions of horsemen and of four horns and craftsmen.
more: Their fathers ignored the prophets, and God's words overtook them.
A man among myrtle trees and other horsemen report that the earth is at rest.
The angel of the LORD intercedes, and God promises compassion and a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem.
Four horns that scattered Judah will be cast down by four craftsmen.

2.line: A man goes to measure Jerusalem, and God promises to be its wall of fire and dwell among his people.
more: Jerusalem will be inhabited without walls because of its many people and livestock.
Exiles are called to flee Babylon, for whoever touches them touches the apple of God's eye.
Many nations will join themselves to the LORD in that day.
Judah will be God's portion in the holy land, and all flesh is called to be silent.

3.line: Joshua the high priest stands accused by Satan, but God removes his filthy garments and promises his servant the Branch.
more: The LORD rebukes Satan, calling Joshua a brand plucked from the fire.
Joshua's filthy garments are replaced with pure vestments and a clean turban.
If Joshua walks in God's ways, he will rule God's house.
A stone with seven eyes is set before him, and God will remove the land's iniquity in one day.

4.line: Zechariah sees a golden lampstand and two olive trees, and learns that Zerubbabel will finish the temple by God's Spirit.
more: The work will succeed not by might or power but by God's Spirit.
Zerubbabel laid the temple's foundation and will complete it.
No one should despise the day of small things.
The two olive trees are two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of all the earth.

5.line: Zechariah sees a flying scroll of curses and a woman in a basket representing wickedness carried away to Shinar.
more: The huge scroll curses thieves and those who swear falsely.
It will enter and consume their houses.
A woman called Wickedness sits in a basket with a lead cover.
Two winged women carry the basket to Shinar to set it in a house there.

6.line: Zechariah sees four chariots patrolling the earth, then crowns Joshua as a sign of the Branch who will build the temple.
more: The chariots come out between two bronze mountains and go to the four winds.
Those going north set God's Spirit at rest in the north country.
The Branch will build the LORD's temple and rule as a priest on his throne.
Those from far away will help build, if the people diligently obey.

7.line: Asked whether to continue fasting, God tells the people that he desires justice and mercy, which their fathers refused.
more: Men from Bethel ask whether they should still mourn and fast in the fifth month.
God asks whether their fasts over seventy years were truly for him.
He calls for true justice, kindness, and care for widows, orphans, sojourners, and the poor.
Their fathers hardened their hearts, so God scattered them and the land became desolate.

8.line: God promises to return to Zion, restore Jerusalem's peace and prosperity, and turn fasts into joyful feasts.
more: Old men and women will sit in Jerusalem's streets, and children will play there.
God will save his people and be their God in faithfulness and righteousness.
They must speak truth, judge justly, and not plot evil.
Many nations will come to seek the LORD, having heard that God is with Judah.

9.line: God announces judgment on Israel's neighbors and the coming of Zion's king, humble and riding on a donkey.
more: Hadrach, Damascus, Tyre, and Philistia will be judged, and a remnant of Philistia will join God's people.
Zion's king is righteous and brings salvation, and he will speak peace to the nations.
Because of the covenant blood, God will free prisoners from the waterless pit.
The LORD will appear over his people, defend them, and save them like a flock.

10.line: God will care for his flock, strengthen Judah, save Joseph, and gather his scattered people home.
more: People should ask the LORD for rain, not household gods and diviners.
God is angry with the shepherds and will make Judah like a warhorse.
From Judah will come the cornerstone, the tent peg, and the battle bow.
He will whistle for his people and bring them back from Egypt and Assyria.

11.line: Zechariah acts as a shepherd for a flock doomed to slaughter, is rejected and paid thirty shekels, and breaks his staffs.
more: Lebanon's cedars and Bashan's oaks wail as destruction comes.
The shepherd takes two staffs, Favor and Union, and removes three shepherds.
He throws his wage of thirty pieces of silver to the potter in the house of the LORD.
God will raise up a worthless shepherd who neglects the flock.

12.line: God will make Jerusalem a cup of staggering for attacking nations, and the people will mourn for the one they pierced.
more: Jerusalem will be a heavy stone that injures all who lift it.
God will strengthen Judah's clans and protect Jerusalem's inhabitants.
He will pour out a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy on David's house.
Each family will mourn bitterly, as one mourns for an only child.

13.line: God will open a fountain to cleanse sin, remove idols and false prophets, and strike the shepherd to refine a remnant.
more: The fountain will cleanse David's house and Jerusalem from sin and uncleanness.
False prophets will be ashamed, and their own parents will oppose them.
When the shepherd is struck, the sheep will scatter.
A third will be refined through fire, and they will call on God's name.

14.line: On the day of the LORD, nations attack Jerusalem, the LORD fights for it, and he becomes king over all the earth.
more: The LORD will stand on the Mount of Olives, and it will split in two.
Living waters will flow from Jerusalem, and there will be continuous day.
The nations that fought against Jerusalem will be struck with plague.
Survivors will worship at the Feast of Booths, and everything will be holy to the LORD.

Malachi.line: Malachi confronts the returned community for dishonoring God and announces a coming day of judgment and healing.
more: The book follows a pattern of God's statement, the people's objection, and God's answer.
God affirms his love for Israel and rebukes priests for offering blemished sacrifices.
He condemns faithlessness in marriage, injustice, and robbing God in tithes.
He promises his messenger and the Lord's coming to his temple to refine and judge.
The book closes by calling Israel to remember Moses' law and promising Elijah's coming.

1.line: God affirms his love for Israel and rebukes the priests for despising his name with blemished offerings.
more: God shows his love by choosing Jacob and bringing Edom's land to ruin.
Priests offer blind, lame, and sick animals they would not give a governor.
God would rather the temple doors be shut than accept such worship.
His name will be great among the nations, from sunrise to sunset.

2.line: God warns the priests for corrupting his covenant with Levi and rebukes Judah for faithlessness and divorce.
more: Priests should teach true instruction, but they have caused many to stumble.
Judah has profaned the covenant by marrying the daughters of foreign gods.
God witnesses against men who break faith with the wife of their youth.
The people weary God by saying evildoers are good in his sight.

3.line: God promises to send his messenger and come to his temple to refine and judge, and calls Israel to return.
more: The Lord will purify the sons of Levi like a refiner's fire.
He will judge sorcerers, adulterers, liars, and oppressors of workers, widows, and orphans.
The people rob God by withholding tithes, and he challenges them to test him.
Those who fear the LORD are written in a book of remembrance as his treasured possession.

4.line: The day of the LORD will burn up the arrogant, but healing will rise for those who fear his name.
more: The sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings.
Those who fear God will tread down the wicked.
Israel is told to remember the law of Moses given at Horeb.
God will send Elijah before the great day to turn the hearts of fathers and children.

Matthew.line: Matthew presents Jesus as the promised Messiah and King, recounting his teaching, death, and resurrection, and his commission to make disciples.
more: Jesus' genealogy, birth, and early life fulfill Old Testament promises.
After his baptism and temptation, he preaches the kingdom of heaven and heals in Galilee.
Five major teaching sections include the Sermon on the Mount and parables of the kingdom.
Opposition grows as Jesus goes to Jerusalem, where he confronts religious leaders and foretells the future.
He is betrayed, crucified, and raised, then sends his disciples to all nations.

1.line: Matthew traces Jesus' genealogy from Abraham through David and tells how Jesus was born of the virgin Mary.
more: The genealogy runs through the exile, arranged in three sets of fourteen generations.
Mary is found to be with child from the Holy Spirit before marrying Joseph.
An angel tells Joseph in a dream to take Mary as his wife and name the child Jesus.
This fulfills Isaiah's prophecy of Immanuel, meaning God with us.

2.line: Wise men worship the child Jesus, and Joseph flees with his family to Egypt to escape Herod.
more: Wise men from the east follow a star to Bethlehem and give gifts.
Herod, feeling threatened, orders the killing of Bethlehem's boys two years old and under.
After Herod dies, Joseph returns and settles the family in Nazareth of Galilee.
Matthew notes that these events fulfill prophecy.

3.line: John the Baptist preaches repentance in the wilderness and baptizes Jesus, and God declares Jesus his beloved Son.
more: John announces that the kingdom of heaven is at hand and baptizes in the Jordan.
He warns Pharisees and Sadducees to bear fruit in keeping with repentance.
He says one mightier will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire.
As Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends on him like a dove.

4.line: Jesus resists the devil's temptations in the wilderness, begins preaching in Galilee, and calls his first disciples.
more: After fasting forty days, he answers each temptation by quoting Scripture.
After John's arrest, Jesus moves to Capernaum and preaches repentance and the kingdom.
He calls Peter, Andrew, James, and John from fishing to follow him.
He heals many, and great crowds follow him.

5.line: Jesus begins the Sermon on the Mount with the Beatitudes and teaches a righteousness deeper than outward law-keeping.
more: He blesses the poor in spirit, mourners, the meek, the merciful, and the persecuted.
His followers are salt and light, and he came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets.
He addresses anger, lust, divorce, oaths, and retaliation at the level of the heart.
He commands love for enemies, to be perfect as the heavenly Father is perfect.

6.line: Jesus teaches that giving, prayer, and fasting should be done for God, not for show, and that disciples should not worry.
more: He gives the Lord's Prayer as a model, stressing forgiveness of others.
Treasures should be stored in heaven, since no one can serve God and money.
The Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies, so his children need not be anxious.
Disciples should seek first God's kingdom and his righteousness.

7.line: Jesus concludes the Sermon on the Mount, warning against judging, false prophets, and hearing his words without doing them.
more: Disciples should remove the log from their own eye before judging others.
God gives good things to those who ask, and the golden rule sums up the Law.
The narrow gate leads to life, and false prophets are known by their fruit.
The wise build their house on the rock by obeying Jesus, and the crowds marvel at his authority.

8.line: Jesus heals a leper, a centurion's servant, and many others, calms a storm, and casts demons into pigs.
more: He praises the Roman centurion's faith as greater than any in Israel.
He heals Peter's mother-in-law and tells would-be followers the cost of discipleship.
The disciples marvel when the wind and sea obey him.
In the Gadarene region, demons enter a herd of pigs, and the townspeople beg Jesus to leave.

9.line: Jesus forgives and heals a paralytic, calls Matthew, raises a girl, and heals many, while Pharisees object.
more: He eats with tax collectors and sinners, saying he came to call sinners.
He explains why his disciples do not fast while he is with them.
He heals a bleeding woman, two blind men, and a mute man.
Seeing the harassed crowds, he asks his disciples to pray for laborers for the harvest.

10.line: Jesus sends out the twelve apostles to preach and heal, preparing them for rejection and persecution.
more: He names the twelve and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel.
They are to travel without provisions and shake off the dust where rejected.
They will be hated and brought before rulers, but they should not fear.
Whoever loses his life for Jesus' sake will find it, and receiving them is receiving him.

11.line: Jesus answers John the Baptist's question, rebukes unrepentant towns, and invites the weary to come to him for rest.
more: He points to his miracles and preaching as signs of who he is.
He calls John more than a prophet, the Elijah who was to come.
Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum are condemned for not repenting despite his mighty works.
The Father reveals these things to little children, and Jesus offers his easy yoke.

12.line: Jesus claims lordship over the Sabbath, heals, and answers Pharisees who accuse him of casting out demons by Beelzebul.
more: He defends his disciples for plucking grain and heals a withered hand on the Sabbath.
The Pharisees plot to destroy him, and he withdraws, fulfilling Isaiah's servant prophecy.
He warns that blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven and offers only the sign of Jonah.
Those who do the Father's will are his brother, sister, and mother.

13.line: Jesus teaches the crowds in parables about the kingdom of heaven and is rejected in his hometown of Nazareth.
more: The parable of the sower shows different responses to the word of the kingdom.
The weeds and the net picture a final separation of the righteous and the wicked.
The mustard seed and leaven show the kingdom's growth, and the treasure and pearl show its worth.
Nazareth takes offense, and he does few mighty works there because of their unbelief.

14.line: After Herod beheads John the Baptist, Jesus feeds five thousand men and walks on the sea.
more: Herod had imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to Herodias.
Jesus multiplies five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over.
Peter walks on the water toward Jesus but begins to sink when he becomes afraid.
The disciples worship Jesus as the Son of God, and many in Gennesaret are healed.

15.line: Jesus rebukes the Pharisees' traditions, heals a Canaanite woman's daughter, and feeds four thousand men.
more: He teaches that defilement comes from the heart, not from unwashed hands.
He grants the Canaanite woman's request because of her great faith.
He heals the lame, blind, and mute by the Sea of Galilee.
Seven loaves and a few fish feed the crowd, with seven baskets left over.

16.line: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, and Jesus begins foretelling his death and resurrection and the cost of following him.
more: Jesus refuses the Pharisees and Sadducees a sign and warns against their leaven.
He says he will build his church on this rock and gives Peter the keys of the kingdom.
He rebukes Peter for opposing his path to suffering.
Disciples must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow him.

17.line: Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, then heals a demon-possessed boy and pays the temple tax.
more: Moses and Elijah appear, and a voice declares Jesus God's beloved Son.
Jesus explains that Elijah has already come in John the Baptist.
The disciples could not heal the boy because of their little faith.
Jesus again foretells his death, and Peter finds a coin in a fish's mouth for the tax.

18.line: Jesus teaches about humility, care for little ones, restoring a sinning brother, and forgiving without limit.
more: Whoever humbles himself like a child is greatest in the kingdom.
The Father seeks the one lost sheep, and causing little ones to sin is serious.
A sinning brother should be approached privately, then with witnesses, then before the church.
The parable of the unforgiving servant warns those who refuse to forgive others.

19.line: Jesus teaches about marriage and divorce, blesses children, and tells a rich young man to sell all and follow him.
more: He points to creation, saying no one should separate what God has joined.
He welcomes little children, for the kingdom belongs to such as these.
The rich man leaves sorrowful, and Jesus says salvation is impossible with man but possible with God.
Those who leave everything for him will receive much and inherit eternal life.

20.line: Jesus tells of vineyard workers paid equally, foretells his death, teaches servant leadership, and heals two blind men.
more: The landowner pays all the workers the same, showing that the last will be first.
The mother of James and John asks for places of honor for her sons.
Jesus came not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom.
Near Jericho, two blind men call out to him and receive their sight.

21.line: Jesus enters Jerusalem as king, clears the temple, curses a fig tree, and tells parables against the religious leaders.
more: Crowds spread cloaks and branches and shout hosanna as he rides a donkey.
He drives out the money-changers and heals the blind and lame in the temple.
Challenged about his authority, he asks the leaders about John's baptism.
Parables of two sons and wicked tenants show the leaders rejecting God's messengers.

22.line: Jesus tells the parable of the wedding feast and silences opponents' questions about taxes, resurrection, and the greatest commandment.
more: Invited guests refuse the king's feast, so others are brought in.
He says to give Caesar what is Caesar's and God what is God's.
He tells the Sadducees there is no marriage in the resurrection and God is God of the living.
The greatest commandments are to love God and neighbor, and he asks whose son the Christ is.

23.line: Jesus denounces the scribes and Pharisees with seven woes for hypocrisy and laments over Jerusalem.
more: They teach but do not practice, and they love honor and titles.
He condemns them for neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness while tithing spices.
They are like whitewashed tombs and will bear guilt for killing the prophets.
He longs to gather Jerusalem like a hen but says its house is left desolate.

24.line: Jesus foretells the temple's destruction, coming tribulation, and his return, and urges his disciples to stay ready.
more: He warns of false christs, wars, famines, and persecution.
The abomination of desolation will bring great tribulation, and those in Judea must flee.
The Son of Man will come on the clouds with power and great glory.
No one knows the day or hour, so the faithful servant must be found ready.

25.line: Jesus tells parables of ten virgins and the talents, and describes the Son of Man judging the nations.
more: Wise virgins with oil enter the wedding feast, but the foolish are shut out.
Servants who invested their master's talents are rewarded, while the one who hid his is cast out.
The Son of Man will separate people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.
Serving the least of his brothers counts as serving him, leading to eternal life or eternal punishment.

26.line: Jesus is anointed, shares the Last Supper, prays in Gethsemane, is arrested, tried by the council, and denied by Peter.
more: The chief priests plot to kill Jesus, and Judas agrees to betray him for thirty pieces of silver.
At the Passover, Jesus gives the bread and cup as his body and his covenant blood.
In Gethsemane he prays for the Father's will to be done while the disciples sleep.
Before Caiaphas he affirms he is the Christ and is condemned for blasphemy.

27.line: Jesus is handed to Pilate, condemned, mocked, and crucified, and after his death he is buried in Joseph's tomb.
more: Judas regrets his betrayal, returns the silver, and hangs himself.
Pilate releases Barabbas at the crowd's demand and hands Jesus over to be crucified.
Darkness covers the land, Jesus cries out and dies, and the temple curtain tears in two.
Guards seal and watch the tomb at the request of the chief priests.

28.line: Jesus rises from the dead, appears to the women and disciples, and commissions them to make disciples of all nations.
more: An angel rolls away the stone and tells the women that Jesus has risen.
The guards report to the chief priests, who bribe them to say the body was stolen.
Jesus meets the eleven on a mountain in Galilee and claims all authority.
He commands them to baptize and teach, promising to be with them always.
